meaning: to have to start planning or working on something again because the first attempt failed
example: The experiment failed, so we are back to the drawing board.
origin: Probably comes from designers who had to return to their drawing boards to redo a plan after it did not work

wrong_meanings.meaning: to draw a picture in a notebook
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: This takes the words literally, but the idiom is about starting a plan again, not about drawing
The idiom describes a failure and a restart, so it is the opposite of finishing successfully
The idiom has nothing to do with becoming an artist; it refers to beginning a task again

explanation: 'Back to the drawing board' means that a plan or idea has failed and we must start again from the beginning. It is often used in science, research and design when an experiment or test does not give the expected result.
